v 68–69 GBM 3315 14r 173 1348 69–70 + Colophon and beginning of the *Kapphiṇa-avadāna* 14v 174 1349 *Kapphiṇa-avadāna*
(Viśv 1) Listen again to how he was ungrateful and lacked awareness of what had been done for him.

(Viśv 2) Long ago, monks, in the capital city of Viśvapuri, a king named Viśvāmitra reigned; his kingdom was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people, and it was free from strife, quarrels, tumults, riots, thieves, and diseases.
It was abundant with rice, sugarcane, cattle, and buffalo. A righteous king, a ruler of dharma, governed the kingdom according to dharma.

That king was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intention; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of dharma, and affectionate toward his subjects.
At another time, he sported, dallied, and enjoyed himself with his queen. While he was thus sporting, dallying, and enjoying himself, after some time, the queen became pregnant.
(Viśv 4) After the passing of eight or nine months, she gave birth. A boy was born, handsome, beautiful,
pleasing, fair-skinned, golden-hued, with a head shaped like a parasol, long arms, a broad forehead, joined eyebrows, a prominent nose,
and endowed with all major and minor limbs.

(5) When he was born, a birth festival was held for him, and his name was established. His kinsmen asked, "What shall be the name of this boy? They said, "Since this boy is the son of King Viśvāmitra, let the boy’s name be Viśvantara. Thus, the name Viśvantara was established for him.
(Viśv 6) The boy Viśvantara was entrusted to eight nurses: two to carry him on their shoulders, two to provide milk, two to clean his impurities, and two to play with him.
He was raised and nourished by these eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, the scum of clarified butter, and other [nutritive foods].
He grew rapidly through excellent, highly refined articles of enjoyment, like a lotus in a pond.
When he had become mature, he was introduced to writing, arithmetic, calculation, and finger-reckoning.
He mastered those skills which belong to anointed Kṣatriya kings who have attained sovereignty, power, and valor over their realms.
For those who dwell having conquered the great circle of the earth, there arise various fields of craft and fields of action,
such as: on the neck of an elephant, on the back of a horse, in a chariot, in swordsmanship, in archery, in retreating, in advancing, in wielding the goad,
in wielding the lasso, in wielding the javelin, in cutting, in splitting, in piercing, in hand-binding, in foot-binding, in hair-binding, and in long-distance shooting.

Prince Viśvantara became an expert in five areas: hitting a sound, hitting a vital point, hitting an eye, and firmness of strike. He was faithful, auspicious, and of noble intent; he was dedicated to his own welfare and the welfare of others, compassionate, magnanimous, a lover of Dharma, affectionate toward his subjects, a giver of all things, a renouncer of all things, and one who renounces everything without attachment.
He abides in great generosity; having heard of the extent of his giving, seekers come from as far as a hundred *yojanas*. He sends them all away with their desires completely fulfilled.
Then, on one occasion, the Bodhisattva [prepared] that which was illuminated by jewels, gold, silver, diamonds, coral, beryl, *musāragalva*, *arkendranīla*, and other gems.

Having mounted an excellent chariot— fitted with the finest heartwood of sandalwood, covered with the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, and yoked to four horses equal in speed to the force of the wind and filling the air with the tinkling of bells made of gold, silver, and jewels—
he departed from the city toward the park.

(Viśv 10) Then, certain Brahmins employed by his adversaries—learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas—approached Prince Viśvantara with great haste and said, "Victory to you, O Kṣatriya prince! And he replied:
"In all the worlds, indeed, you are renowned as one who gives everything."
You ought to give this chariot as a gift to the twice-born.

(Viśv 11) When this had been said, the Bodhisattva, having swiftly descended from that excellent chariot with a heart thrilled, satisfied, and gladdened, spoke to those twice-born ones while pointing out that excellent chariot: "Just as this chariot has been given by me to the brahmins with supreme joy,"
In that same way, having abandoned the three realms of existence, may I touch supreme enlightenment.

(Viśv 12) At another time, he mounted the preeminent elephant named Rājyavardhana—the color of which was like jasmine, the kumuda lily, snow, silver, or white clouds; whose seven well-formed feet were firmly planted upon the ground; who moved with the graceful gait of the elephant Airāvaṇa; who was adorned with the natural marks of excellence; and who was a joy to behold—and set forth, surrounded by contented servants, friends, attendants, and followers, like the moon encircled by a host of stars.
When the season of spring had arrived and the trees were in full bloom, with the forest groves resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, jīvañjīvas, and vakas,
he went out to the garden grounds. Then, certain brahmins dispatched by his enemies— who were learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas— approached Prince Viśvantara very hurriedly and said:
"Victory to you, O Kṣatriya prince! he said;
"and you, who are renowned throughout the worlds of the Daityas and the gods as the Giver of All, you ought to grant this excellent elephant to us here."

(14) When this had been said, the Bodhisattva, having very quickly descended even from that excellent elephant, with a mind joyful, contented, and delighted, pointed out that excellent elephant to those twice-born ones, saying:
"Just as I have given this elephant to the brahmins with supreme joy,
so may I, having abandoned the three worlds, touch supreme enlightenment."
(Viśv 15) King Viśvāmitra heard that his son Viśvantara had given away the excellent elephant named Rājyavardhana to Brahmins employed by his enemies. Upon hearing this, King Viśvāmitra,
provoked to the highest pitch of anger, summoned Prince Viśvantara and said to him:
"Go, prince; you must not dwell within my domain.
Abandoned by his father, the prince reflected:
"By me, who have resolved upon awakening and donned the armor for the sake of benefiting all the world, this elephant has been released."
While residing in that house, one should give gifts according to one's ability;
or else, having retired to a penance grove, one should observe the highest discipline.
Therefore, having abandoned my home, I shall depart for the forest of asceticism;
however, I cannot bring myself to speak the words "I will not give" to a supplicant.
(Viśv 17) Then, having thus resolved his mind, the Bodhisattva approached his wife Mādrī and informed her of this in detail.
Upon hearing it, Mādrī’s heart was immediately struck with the fear of being separated from her beloved; joining her palms in reverence, she said to the Bodhisattva:
"Noble Son, if that is so, I too shall go to the forest of asceticism. Separated from my Noble Son, I am not able to sustain my life for even a moment. Why is that?"
Just as the sky is without the moon, or as the earth may be without its crops,
or as a lotus pond is without water, so too is a woman without her husband.
The Bodhisattva said:

"Inevitably, at the end, there must be separation for us both; for such is the nature of the world. You, moreover, have been nurtured with the finest food, drink, bedding, seats, and clothing, and your body is exceedingly delicate. Yet, in the forest of asceticism, you must sleep upon ground covered only with grass and leaves."

Your food shall consist of roots, flowers, and fruits; you must wander upon the earth strewn with *darbha* grass, stones, *kuśa* grass, and thorns; you must frequently observe the fast; you must present yourself before all people;
and with every effort, you must honor guests. Even in that state, I must certainly give gifts according to my ability. Regarding this, you must not feel any regret whatsoever. Furthermore—
"Let this first be considered," he said.
Mādrī replied, "Noble son, I shall follow the noble son to the best of my ability.
The Bodhisattva said, "If that is so, you must remember this promise."
(Viśv 19) Then the Bodhisattva, having approached his father and prostrated with his head at his feet, said:
"Forgive me, O Father, for whatever offense I have committed regarding the gift of the elephant, O Lord of Kings.
I shall depart from this city for the forest; let there be no depletion of your treasury, O King. Thus he spoke.
Then the king, distressed by the separation from his son, his voice faltering as it was choked with tears, said:
"Son, stay! Let your mind be turned away from this gift. The Bodhisattva replied:
"Even though the earth, together with its mountains, might turn back..."
O Lord of the Earth, I shall not turn my mind away from giving.
Having said this, he departed.

(Viśv 20) Then, accompanied by his sons, daughters, and wife, and followed by hundreds of thousands of citizens and countryfolk who were overcome with grief and longing, he mounted a chariot and went out from that excellent city.
(Viśv 21) Now, a certain man, having heard that sound of weeping and lamentation and seeing the great multitude of people departing through the city gate, spoke to another man:
"O man, what is the cause of this sound of weeping from the great multitude?
He replied, "Do you not know? That our own king has sent his son, Sudamṣṭra, away from our country..."
Firm in resolve and devoted to giving,
he who is destined for nirvana has departed for the forest with his son and wife;
and the citizens and servants weep most piteously.

(Viśv 22) Then the Bodhisattva Viśvantara, having approached the citizens who had come out from that excellent city in the prescribed manner, said: "Turn back, turn back, sirs! For even a very long association with loved ones must necessarily end in separation at the conclusion. Even for one who serves as a tree of rest on the road of existence, separation from kinsmen is inevitable."
There is separation from what is dear. Why?

Because it is understood that in all worlds, a living being inevitably experiences separation from those dear to him; therefore, you must, with every effort on this earth, cultivate a firm and unshakable intellect for the sake of tranquility.
(Viśv 23) Then, seeing the Bodhisattva who had traveled thirty yojanas, a certain brahmin approached and said:

"O Kṣatriya prince, there is a city some thirty yojanas from here, for which I have come because I have heard of your virtues. Therefore, you ought to make my labor fruitful by accepting this excellent chariot."
Then Mādrī, filled with indignation, spoke to that brahmin with harsh words:
"Aha! How cruel is this twice-born man's mind, that even in the forest he makes such a request of the prince;
surely no compassion arises in him for the son of a king who has been deprived of royal splendor."
The Bodhisattva said: "Indeed, indeed, you must not revile the brahmin. Why?
Because, O Mādrī, if these recipients who provide for one's needs were not present,"
What man on earth could attain awakening without giving everything?
Bodhisattvas of supreme virtue always attain unsurpassed omniscience with certainty through the six perfections, beginning with generosity.

(Viśv 24) Then the Bodhisattva, with supreme joy, gave even that horse-chariot to the brahmin and said: "O twice-born one, by this gift of a chariot— which washes away the stain of stinginess regarding food— may I here obtain the great, stainless chariot made of Dharma, which was set in motion by the six Great Sages."
(Viśv 25) Then the Bodhisattva, with a joyful heart, gave even that excellent chariot to the brahmin;
placing the maiden Kṛṣṇājinā upon his shoulder and Mādrī along with the prince Jālin, they set out toward the forest of asceticism.
In due course, they arrived at the forest of asceticism. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Viśvantara, in that forest of asceticism, [found] that which brings satisfaction to his own heart—
Having undertaken the vow, he lived there.
Now at that time, a certain brahmin was living in a particular mountain village. He had brought home a wife from a family of equal status. He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her.
While he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born who was endowed with eighteen inauspicious marks. When he ran about, the name Jujjuka, Jujjuka came to be given to him.

(Viśv 27) In a certain mountain village there lived a brahmin who was learned in the four Vedas. He brought home a wife from a family of equal status. While he was sporting, enjoying himself, and dallying with her, a daughter was born to him—beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing—within the space of four days.
She grew up to be a young woman. That brahmin made this vow:
"I shall not give this daughter of mine to anyone on account of her beauty, her lineage, her wealth, or her artistic skill; rather, she must be given by me to whoever learns the four Vedas from me."
(Viśv 28) Then Jujjuka, seeking mantras and searching for mantras, approached his house. He was addressed by that brahmin:
"O young man, from where have you come, or what do you seek?
He replied: "I wish to perform service at the feet of the preceptor."
He said, "Excellent, young man, do so; this is what must be done by brahmins.
He began to study the Vedas in his presence. Being naturally intelligent, he mastered the four Vedas in a very short time.

(Viśv 30) That Brahmin reflected: "I have made a vow that this daughter of mine must not be given to anyone on account of her beauty, or her lineage, or her wealth, or her skill; rather, she must be given to whoever shall master the four Vedas from me."
"This young brahmin has acquired the four Vedas from me, yet he is possessed of eighteen inauspicious marks. It would be excellent if he were to accept this girl.
He said this to him. (Viśv 31)
"O young brahmin, a vow was made by me that this daughter of mine is not to be given away to anyone on account of her beauty, her lineage, her wealth, or her craft;
rather, she is to be given to whoever shall master the four Vedas from me. And you have mastered the four Vedas from me. Therefore, I give my daughter to you for the sake of a wife.
He said:
"May there be well-being; let her be accepted.
He then had a marriage performed for him with that great abundance of splendor, and having done so, he said:
"Young man, take your wife and go to your own home."
(Viśv 32) Taking his wife, he went to his own home. She said to him:
"Noble son, I am delicate; I am unable to perform manual labor. Please grant me an attendant.
He replied:
"My lady, where am I to find an attendant?
She replied, "Noble son, in Viśvapuri there is a king named Viśvāmitra. He has a son named Viśvantara who gives whatever is asked of him. Seek an attendant for me from his presence."
He said:
"Noble lady, if that is so, let us go together.
Having gone with her to Viśvapuri, he asked:
"Where is Prince Viśvantara?
They replied,
"He has retired to a forest of asceticism."
(Viśv 34) Then Jujjuka went to the forest of asceticism together with his wife.
(Viśv 35) Thereupon, that brahmin, having come out from the forest of asceticism to meet Mādrī who had gone there for the sake of roots and fruits, approached Viśvantara and said:
"May you be victorious, O prince!"
(40) He reported the matter thus:
"Surely my two young sons, who delight the eyes and are charming, have gone to the forest of asceticism subsisting on fruits and water;
it is for the sake of liberating the world from suffering that Viśvaṃtara renounces them, because of which the earth trembles."

(Viśv 41) Then those two young children, perceiving their father’s intention to renounce them, wept most piteously; falling at the feet of Viśvantara with palms joined in supplication, they said: "Be gracious, dear father, do not abandon us! Deprived of our elders, we shall perish.
Mother has already departed, dear father, and you ought not to give us away as well."
Once we have seen her as well, then you shall give her to us.

Then the Bodhisattva, his heart filled with distress and his face bathed in tears, embraced those two young children and said: "My sons, it is not that my heart is unaffectionate, nor lacking in compassion, nor devoid of tenderness;
rather, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world, I relinquish you both, who behold such virtues."
Having myself awakened to supreme, auspicious enlightenment,
may I ferry across the world— which has fallen into the ocean of suffering and is without refuge— to the further shore.

(Viśv 42) Then those two young boys, perceiving their father’s intention to renounce them, fell at his feet with words slow and piteous with compassion; joining their palms in reverence, they said: "If this is your resolve, then on our behalf you must speak to our mother, dear father; O mother, you ought to forgive us here."
Moreover, dear one, whatever offense we have committed against our guru because of our childishness toward you, or if anything unpleasant was ever uttered by us;
Even if it were not fully satisfied by service, that would still be a fault of the fool; therefore, it must indeed be forgiven.

Having spoken thus, and having saluted his father, he circumambulated him three times. Keeping the words of their teacher in mind, they turned back again and again, their eyes overflowing with tears. Then, his heart overwhelmed by those most piteous words of the young children, the Bodhisattva fixed his mind upon awakening and departed for the practice of austerities. And as soon as those two young children had gone forth, [the Bodhisattva left] from that hermitage.
This trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and from the sky there arose the cry of "Ha! Ha! from many thousands of deities:
"Oh, the greatness of this gift! Oh, the resolve of this being!"
That my mind is not overcome with grief even after abandoning these two young sons—[this is truly extraordinary].

(Viśv 44) At that time, Mādrī, having taken roots and fruits, set out toward the hermitage. Because of that great earthquake, she proceeded toward the hermitage with extreme haste. There, a certain deity, assuming the form of a lion, stood blocking the path so that Mādrī would not [approach] the Bodhisattva.

"Thinking that she would create an obstacle for me as I am striving for the liberation of all sentient beings in the perfection of generosity," Mādrī then said to that woman who was sporting like the mate of a king of deer:
"O you who sport like the mate of a king of deer, why do you stand here obstructing me?"
Since I am certainly destined for my husband, move quickly away from my path.
Moreover,
you are the wife of the king of beasts, and I too am the wife of the lion among kings;
by right, O queen of beasts, you are my sister, so give me passage.
When she had spoken thus, that deity in the form of a lion departed from that path.
Then Mādrī, perceiving that these were ill-omened signs, reflected for a moment:
"Just as this sound of weeping is heard in the sky..."
And as the sound of the forest-dwelling creatures fleeing clearly indicates that some misfortune will occur at the hermitage, he said:
"From the way my eye throbs, from the way the bird cries,
from how our two children have been left behind, and from how my mind is so anxious."
Just as this earth trembles, so does my heart; it is evident that the two children have been abandoned, for even my body is sinking.

(Viśv 46) Thus reflecting on hundreds of thousands of misfortunes, she went to the hermitage; having entered the hermitage, she looked about in agitation but did not see those two sons. Then Mādrī, with a distressed heart and trembling, reasoned according to their usual haunts:
"In this place, the prince used to play constantly with his sister and the young deer. These...
And they have built sand-castles with those two; these are their playthings, yet I do not see them. Or perhaps, thinking "Mother is not seen," they have entered the leaf-hut and are lying down.
Thus, her heart overwhelmed by such apprehension and longing to see her sons, she set aside the roots and fruits in a secluded spot.
With her eyes overflowing with tears, she fell at her husband’s feet and asked, "Noble son, where have those two young children gone?
Viśvantara replied,
"A brahmin approached me with hope."
Those two boys have been given to him; you ought to grant them permission.

(Viśv 48) Then, having been addressed in this way, Mādrī fell to the ground like a doe pierced by a poisoned arrow. Like a fish pulled from its watery home, she rolled and writhed upon the earth. Like a female osprey whose young has been snatched away, she wailed most piteously. And like a cow that has lost her calf, she lamented with many kinds of lowing cries. And she said:
With faces like young lotuses and hands as delicate as lotus petals, my two little sons—though they have never experienced suffering—are now in pain; to what state of existence have they gone?

How indeed are my two little sons, who were so fond of the hermitage and used to play with the deer— those fawn-eyed boys as gentle as young deer— now suffering today as they must go under the control of another?
With eyes overflowing with tears, lamenting piteously and deeply distressed, they have not been allowed to see me well today; alas, these two miserable ones live in suffering!
These two sons of mine, who have grown up on me, subsisting only on roots, flowers, and fruits,
and always pleasing their elders through patience and gentleness— my two sons are indeed deeply distressed.
Deprived of kinsmen and mother, and suddenly cast out by their relatives,
my two sons have indeed come to live among wicked and sinful people, and are thus suffering most intensely.
Whose control will those two, whose very nature is gripped by hunger and thirst, ever come under?
And being tormented by affliction and suffering, they will certainly fall into a state of servitude.
Surely some very terrible evil karma was committed by me here in another birth, by which I,
an unrighteous being, am separated from hundreds of dear ones and low like a cow, crying out in distress.
By that word of truth through which my mind has always been inclined toward the equality of all sentient beings,
by that word of truth may these two sons of mine be released from their state of servitude.
(Viśv 49) Then Mādrī, seeing those trees which had been planted and nurtured by her two young children now covered in new sprouts, embraced them in agitation and said:
"O child, O child! The shoots, watered like jars, have fallen as teardrops;
the little trees seem to weep with consciousness, like infants deprived of their mother's breast."

(Viśv 50) Furthermore, seeing the young fawns dwelling in the hermitage as playthings for those two children, he spoke these words in syllables faltering with compassion and distress: "This is indeed another great sorrow, that these young fawns take delight [here]; longing for the sight of their companions, they search about in their various haunts."
(Viśv 51) Then Mādrī, following the path by which those two young children had gone, saw their footprints here and there, none of them empty;
struck by intense grief, she spoke again:
"They have surely been led away while being beaten, as can be seen from the uneven spacing of their footprints."
Alas, O cruel one, best of the twice-born, you have gone to some state from which there is no return!
With throats choked by sobs and tears, their beautiful lower lips trembling,
and their eyes darting like those of a deer— how did those two go with their tender little feet?
(Viśv 52) Then the Bodhisattva, seeing them thus lamenting and instructing them in many ways through various teachings connected with impermanence, said:
"It was not out of pride nor out of malice that I abandoned my two sons;
rather, for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, those two sons so difficult to give up were renounced by me."
Having renounced their own bodies, children, and wives— which are most difficult to abandon—
the Great Beings attain supreme enlightenment according to the prescribed method.
"O Mādrī, since you two sons—so difficult to give away—have been surrendered by me as the foundation for renunciation for the sake of the world’s liberation;
therefore, my mind is resolved to give away my own wife, my vehicle, and all my wealth to everyone.
(Viśv 53) Then Mādrī, summoning her fortitude, spoke to the Bodhisattva with her heart.
I shall not create an obstacle for you; let not your mind be otherwise.
If you wish to give me as well, bestow me upon him without hesitation.
Moreover,
O Hero, quickly attain that goal for the sake of which you abandon your own kin who are overwhelmed by affection, and deliver the world from the three realms of existence.

(Viśv 54) Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having understood that most wonderful and exceedingly difficult resolve of Mādrī and the Bodhisattva, surrounded by the hosts of the Thirty-three, approached that hermitage through the upper air. Illuminating that forest with a magnificent radiance, while still stationed in the expanse of the sky, he spoke to the Bodhisattva:

O All-pervading Lord, while the world is deluded, its intellects agitated by evil thoughts, and attached to enjoyments— yet you alone, free from attachment, renounce your son, that source of affection, along with his bonds.
You will surely attain the state that is firm, secure, peaceful, stainless, and free from dust.

(Viśv 55) Having thus encouraged the Bodhisattva, Śakra, the lord of the gods, reflected: "He is alone and without an attendant; he will fall into exhaustion. What if I were also to make a request of him? Then, departing from the presence of the Bodhisattva and assuming the guise of a brahmin, he spoke again to the Bodhisattva.
Give me this woman, whose limbs are entirely faultless, who is devoted to her husband, faithful to her lord, and worthy of praise by her family— she who is to share in the portion of my service.
(Viśv 56) Then Mādrī, filled with indignation, spoke to that brahmin with harsh words:
"O lowest of brahmins, you are both shameless and greedy,
since you desire me, a devoted wife who is dedicated to the true dharma."
(Viśv 57) Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, his heart overwhelmed with compassion, began to look at Mādrī. Then Mādrī said to the Bodhisattva:
"I do not grieve for myself, nor do I have any concern for my own self;
rather, I grieve for you—how will you be alone?"
Then the Bodhisattva said to Mādrī:

"O Mādrī, I am not to be mourned here on earth, for I am seeking the imperishable state free from sorrow. Follow this twice-born man, O Viśokā; as for me, I shall enter the hermitage to take refuge among the deer."
(Viśv 58) Having understood this, with a heart thrilled, satisfied, and joyful, he reflected:
"In this forest, this will be my final act of giving;
having abandoned Mādrī, my beloved, I shall become one who possesses nothing."
Having understood this, he took Mādrī by the hand and said to that brahmin:
"O best of the twice-born, accept this wife of mine as your disciple— she who is devoted to her affectionate service, of virtuous conduct, and sweet-spoken."
(Viśv 59) Then, as he touched his wife with the desire for awakening,
the entire earth shook in six ways, like a boat upon the water.
(Viśv 60) Then Mādrī, her voice choked with tears and her throat faltering, having fallen under the power of the brahmins and being separated from her husband, sons, and daughter, spoke these words:
"What ignoble deed did I commit in previous births,
that like a cow who has lost her calf, I lament here in this desolate forest?"
(Viśv 61) Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, having made his brahmin disguise disappear and standing in his own form, said to Mādrī:
"O fortunate lady, I am not a brahmin, nor am I a human;
I am indeed Śakra, the lord of the gods and the destroyer of the asuras."
"I am pleased with this supreme discipline of yours;
therefore, tell me, what boon do you desire from my presence?"
Then Mādrī, her heart filled with joy by those words, bowed down to Śakra and said:
"O Thousand-eyed One, O Lord of the Thirty-three, release my two sons from their state of servitude and lead them into the presence of the Grandfather."
( Viśv 62) Having said, "So be it," Mahendra entered the hermitage once more and approached the Bodhisattva. Taking Mādrī by his left hand, he said to the Bodhisattva:
"I give this Mādrī to you as an attendant;
she must not be given to anyone else, for the betrayal of a trust is censurable."
(Viśv 63) Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, so utterly bewildered that brahmin who had taken hold of the young boy that,
suspecting it was another city, he approached that very city and began to offer the two young boys for sale;
when this was seen by the ministers, they informed the king.
"These two sons of yours, Jālina and Kṛṣṇā, are being sold by that cruel brahmin in this best of cities."
(Viśv 64) Having heard this, the king, his mind bewildered, said: "Show me the two princes quickly!
The women staying in the inner apartments raised a cry, and the citizens quickly came into the presence of the king.
When one of the ministers brought the two sons before the king, the monarch gazed upon them as they were presented face-to-face—
voices weakened, bodies emaciated, and limbs smeared with filth.
He suddenly fell from the lion-throne onto the surface of the earth;
the citizens, the hosts of ministers, and the women all cried out in lamentation.
(Viśv 65) Then the king addressed his ministers:
"Bring that Sulocana here quickly, together with his wife, whose mind remains devoted to giving even while dwelling in the forest."
(Viśv 66) Thereupon Śakra, the lord of the gods, having paid homage to the Bodhisattva, returned to his own abode.

(Viśv 67) And when King Viśvāmitra had passed away, Śakra, together with the brahmins, ministers, citizens, and countryfolk, went to that hermitage, requested the Bodhisattva [to come], brought him to his own city, and established him on the throne.

(Viśv 68) Thereupon, King Viśvantara became a giver of all things (*sarvadada*). Having bestowed gifts of many kinds upon ascetics, brahmins, beggars, friends, relatives, kinsmen, dependents, and the destitute, and having performed meritorious deeds, he spoke this verse while aspiring for awakening:
"A confident person, desiring awakening, should give gifts."
In a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, a śūdra, and even among caṇḍālas and pukkāsas.
Gold and fine gold, cattle, horses, jewels, and earrings.
Likewise, one should give a servant or laborer to those who are endowed with excellent conduct.
Having renounced their children and wives with a liberated mind,
men attain purity both in this world and in the next.

(Viśv 69) When King Viśvāmitra gave abundant wealth to the brahmin Jujjuka on account of Prince Viśvantara, he became possessed of extensive fortune. His friends, relatives, kinsmen, and companions came to him and said: "Whatever prosperity, good fortune, and excellence you possess, it has all come about because of Prince Viśvantara. He replied:
"What has been done for me by Viśvantara? I am born of the highest caste and am worthy of the world's offerings;
yet he is the one who brings me these enjoyments."
The Blessed One said:

"What do you think, monks? He who was the prince named Viśvantara at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself. He who was the brahmin Jujjuka at that time and on that occasion was none other than Devadatta."

Even then he was ungrateful and failed to recognize what had been done for him; even now he is ungrateful and fails to recognize what has been done for him. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We shall be grateful and we shall acknowledge what has been done for us; we will not let even a small favor go to waste, much less a great one.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The Legend of Viśvantara is completed.
